summary: Catharine Bird Runkle was an Indologist. She studied at Radcliffe College in 1886 under Charles Rockwell Lanman.

Catherine Bell was a scholar in religious studies and sinology. She studied at the University of Chicago under Joseph M. Kitagawa from circa 1976 to 1983 and was the Bernard J. Hanley Professor of Religious Studies at Santa Clara University (1985–2008).

Catherine Cornille works in religious and Buddhist studies. She studied at KU Leuven (Licentiate 1979–1984, Ph.D. 1986–1989) and the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa. She taught at KU Leuven, College of the Holy Cross, and Boston College.

Catherine Ella Blanshard Asher specialized in history, archaeology, and Indology. She completed her PhD at the University of Minnesota circa 1975–1984, where she served as an assistant professor from circa 1984 to 2021.

Catherine Ludvik is a scholar of religious, Buddhist, and Japanese studies. She earned her PhD at the University of Toronto (supervised by David Waterhouse) and held posts at the Italian School of East Asian Studies, Stanford, Doshisha, and Kyoto Sangyo Universities.

Catherine Prueitt is a scholar of philosophy, Indology, and religious studies. She studied at the University of Rochester and Emory University (PhD under John D. Dunne). She held assistant professorships at George Mason University (2017–2019) and the University of British Columbia (2019).
Cathy Cantwell is a scholar of Tibetology and Buddhist studies. She earned her PhD from the University of Kent (circa 1983–1989) and held a post at the University of Oxford in 2002.

Cecil Bendall was an Indologist and Buddhist studies scholar who studied at Cambridge and Göttingen. He held posts at the British Museum, University College London, and the University of Cambridge, serving as Professor of Sanskrit from 1903 to 1906.

Cecil Henry Bompas worked in Indology. He studied at Westminster School and Trinity College, Cambridge, before serving in the Indian Civil Service (1887–1923), the Bengal Legislative Council (1916), and as chairman of the Calcutta Improvement Trust (1920).

Cecil Jermyn Brown worked in history, archaeology, and Indology. After earning an M.A. at Trinity College, Oxford, he taught at Canning College, held a fellowship at the University of Allahabad, and served as Professor of English Literature at the University of Lucknow.

Cecil Y. Lang studied at Duke University before holding academic appointments at Yale University, the University of Chicago, and the University of Virginia, where he served as Professor of English from circa 1970 to 1991.
Cezary Galewicz is an Indologist who served as an adjunct professor (attested 2012) and became a professor in 2015 at Jagiellonian University.

Ch'ing-mao Cheng, a scholar of sinology and japanology, earned degrees from National Taiwan University and Princeton. He taught at UC Berkeley and the University of Massachusetts Amherst, later becoming the Founding Chair at National Dong Hwa University.

Chack-fan Lee, active in Buddhist studies, studied at the University of Hong Kong and the University of Western Ontario. He served as Pro-Vice-Chancellor at the University of Hong Kong from 1994 to 2015.
Chaesong Kim is a scholar of Buddhist studies and Indology. Kim studied doctoral coursework at the University of Tokyo (attested 1995) under Yasunori Ejima.

Chagdud Tulku Rinpoche was a Buddhist studies and Tibetology figure. He studied under teachers including Delog Dawa Drolma, Dudjom Jigdral Yeshe Dorje, Jamyang Khyentse Chökyi Lodrö, Tromge Trungpa Rinpoche, Khenpo Dorje, Jangchub Dorje, and Dilgo Khyentse Rinpoche.

Chaim Rabin was a linguist educated at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, SOAS, and Oxford. He served as a lecturer at SOAS and Oxford before becoming an associate professor at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem (1956–1985).

Chaisit Suwanvarangkul is a scholar of Buddhist studies and philosophy. He held researcher positions at Kyoto University and the University of Delhi, and served as a Lecturer in Buddhist Studies at the University of Otago (attested 2015).

Chakravarthi Ram-Prasad specializes in philosophy, religious studies, and Indology. He earned a doctorate in philosophy from Oxford, held research fellowships at Oxford and Cambridge, and became a Distinguished Professor at Lancaster University.

Chamnong Adivadhanasit works in religious and Buddhist studies, earning a BA from Chulalongkorn University. In 2012, he was attested as a professor at Kasetsart University and a part-time instructor at Chulalongkorn University.
